pillar_reactions.evidence: Engaged closely and asked the questions that mattered to him — 'as a 68 year old, can I benefit from your program? Do you have other 68 or older people?' and, on form video, 'I'm sure that if I don't do it right, not only am I maybe not going to get the benefits, but I could also potentially hurt myself.' He then confirmed: 'Oh yeah, yeah, I think that's all true.'

Accepted without pushback — 'Yeah, yeah, no doubt' — and had already demonstrated the relevant capability by giving up ice cream for Lent and not returning to it. He was open about the gaps himself: 'we also have sodas in the house, cookies in the house, potato chips in the house. I know those are not good' and confirmed it could be daily.

Accepted and specifically valued the form-correction loop: 'the filming of myself so that he could check out my form, I think that's really important.' He framed his own reliability as the reason it would work — 'once I make a commitment to something, I follow through.'

anchors.raw: there was a chiropractor here in town that had a clinic that is only for neuropathy, and I paid, I think it was like $8,000. I'm still paying for that. And it really, I mean, it did help, but I still have the problem... So that was money that I haven't seen, I haven't seen the result.
anchors.note: The most important anchor on this call. He has just spent more than the asking price on a health intervention that did not fix the problem and is still servicing the debt. He then articulated the resulting decision rule himself: 'the most expensive drug is the one that doesn't work.' Every dollar of the $6,000 is being weighed against that memory, and the rep never addressed it.

anchors.raw: I have a bunch of videos saved, which is what I've been doing to work out. I've been working out with kettlebells now for a couple of weeks.
anchors.competitor: Trevor's own free Instagram and YouTube content
anchors.note: He is already training on the provider's free content and reporting that it feels effective — 'I feel the cardio effect. I feel the pump. I see my muscles working.' He also predicted this would be his wife's exact objection: 'you can look up videos and do it.' The rep's counter was a single question, 'but does it make your form better?', which is the right wedge but was asked once and dropped.

anchors.raw: I mean, have you heard of P90X? And I did that. I guess I was like 57 or 58... my wife takes a picture. And I look at the picture and I'm like, Oh my God, I have abs.
anchors.note: A low-cost DVD programme demonstrably produced the aesthetic outcome for him at 57. His stated objection to repeating it is sustainability rather than efficacy, which is the correct angle for the rep to take and he did take it — but the precedent that cheap programmes work on this man is established.

anchors.raw: I don't have the income that I used to have that was coming in. You know, now I'm on a limited budget.
anchors.note: Raised voluntarily fifteen minutes before the price and labelled by him as 'another real objection'. High former income, low current liquidity — the classic preserver profile, and the reason the monthly reframe to '$1,000 a month' did not land.

anchors.raw: It's going to take me 20 minutes to get there, 20 minutes to come back. There goes 40 minutes. And nah, I'm not going to do it.
anchors.note: He has ruled out the cheap default option on grounds of time and environment rather than money, which removes the gym as a comparator and is one of the few anchors working in the offer's favour.

anchors.raw: Initially, oh, too much money. You can look up videos and do it
anchors.note: He supplied his wife's objection verbatim before she had heard the pitch. The person who has to be convinced is not in the room and already holds the free-alternative argument.

unmet_demand.want: Help understanding his medications and what to ask his doctor
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He set this out as the frame for his whole year — 'what kind of changes do I have to make, not only physically with my training, but also with the meds that I'm on... so that I can ask better questions to my doctor' — and it went unanswered. The programme does not and should not do this, and nobody said so, which leaves the expectation live.

unmet_demand.want: Evidence the programme works for people in their late sixties
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He asked directly and got an unnamed 65-year-old and 'I think that always was 75, not 100% sure'. No case study, no numbers, no introduction to an older client. For the prospect this is the central risk question and the answer was anecdotal.

unmet_demand.want: A programme that works around peripheral neuropathy, plantar fasciitis and documented back problems
unmet_demand.why_unmet: There is no clinical screening step and no referral pathway. His conditions were treated as mobility inputs rather than as constraints, and the response was 'those pains are gone' rather than a question about whether he is cleared to load.

He named it as a goal and the rep acknowledged it once as 'a nice goal' before moving on. Nothing in the pillar delivery connected the training to it, and the plantar fasciitis that has actually been blocking it was never revisited.

unmet_demand.want: Something for his wife, who does not train
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised it as a hoped-for second-order outcome — 'hopefully maybe get my wife involved because she doesn't like to train at all' — and there is no partner or household offering. Notably this is also the person who has to approve the purchase.
